headline: Only positions occupied in both trees need addition and further comparison
statement: Merge two binary trees position by position. Where both have a node, sum their values; where only one has a node, retain that node and subtree. Return the merged root. Input nodes may be mutated or reused; an allocating merge is also allowed.
intuition: Visit the two trees at corresponding positions. If both nodes exist, add their values into the first tree. If only one exists, keep that whole branch. Continue comparing overlapping child pairs. This handles missing children without treating them as actual zero-valued nodes.
approach: Return the other root when either input root is absent.
Traverse pairs of overlapping nodes using a stack, adding the second value into the first.
For each child direction, attach the second child if the first is absent; otherwise queue the overlapping pair.
correctness: An overlapping pair receives exactly the sum required for its position. A one-sided subtree already matches every required value below that position and is attached intact. Traversing every overlapping child pair applies this same rule at all remaining positions, producing the merged tree.
bruteForce: Serialize both trees by positions and reconstruct every output node, requiring extra maps and allocations.

complexity.explanation: p is the number of positions occupied in both trees, and h is the maximum depth of that overlapping region. Each paired position is visited once. The DFS pending stack is O(h+1); a one-sided subtree is attached without traversal. The loose whole-input bound is O(n+m).

pitfalls: Check for missing roots before adding values.
This reference reuses/mutates input nodes; the problem allows it.
Do not drop a child that exists only in the second tree.
